items.title: BTR's Indonesian anode plant
items.subtitle: PT Indonesia BTR New Energy Material · Morowali and Kendal, Indonesia
items.question: Could Sayari detect Chinese graphite anode material reaching US battery plants through BTR's plant in Indonesia?
items.headline: Yes for the trade, no for the ownership. Sayari shows dated HS 3801.10 shipments from the Indonesian plant to five US battery and auto makers, and Chinese artificial graphite flowing into the same plant. It does not show who owns the plant. That link comes only from open sources.

steps.title: The corridor
steps.text: Since January 2024, about 47,000 shipments of artificial graphite (HS 3801.10) have reached the US. Spain, China, India, Germany and Morocco lead. Indonesia isn't in the top ten, so a single plant's trail is easy to miss in aggregate data.

steps.title: The plant: five records, one site
steps.text: Sayari holds five separate records for the Indonesian plant. Four share the same Kendal street address and a version of the same name. One has only a Jakarta district and is kept as a lead. We treat them as one plant, labelled Inferred, because no identifier links them.

steps.title: The owner: not in the registry
steps.text: Sayari returns no shareholders for the plant, and its shortest path to BTR in China is a trade link. Sayari does show BTR owning a different Indonesian company (Liyuan), so the gap is specific to this plant. BTR's own press release calls the plant its Indonesian facility, so the ownership edge is shown with that source, not Sayari's.

steps.title: Same product in, same product out
steps.text: Artificial graphite (HS 3801) arrives from BTR and from a trader registered in the BTR Building in Shenzhen. Artificial graphite (HS 3801.10) leaves for Ultium Cells, SK Battery America, StarPlus Energy, GM and Tesla, Dec 2024 to Aug 2025. Natural graphite also arrives from Mozambique, Madagascar and the UAE.

steps.title: Where the trail goes dark
steps.text: Trade records can't show which input went into which export, so Chinese-origin content can't be measured. Supplier rollups by HS code returned 0, and two name filters were silently ignored. Battery-maker shipments in our results stop after Aug 2025; later rows go to industrial buyers. We haven't tested why.

detected.text: Dated HS 3801.10 shipments from the Indonesian plant to Ultium Cells (Warren and Spring Hill), SK Battery America, StarPlus Energy, GM and Tesla, Dec 2024 – Aug 2025.
Artificial graphite (HS 3801) shipped into the plant from China by BTR and by a trader registered in the BTR Building, Dec 2023 – Jun 2026.
Five fragmented Sayari records for one plant, four of them tied by a shared street address.

suggested.text: Chinese parent ownership: the parent's name, a trade link and BTR's own press release point the same way, but Sayari has no registry record of it.
A same-group trading arm: Shenzhen Ruiqing shares the BTR Building address and is the plant's busiest graphite shipper.
Forced-labor exposure: sub-tier flags on the plant come through 'possibly the same as' paths; the parent is named in Sheffield Hallam forced-labor reports (per Sayari).

not_visible.text: Who owns the plant, and in what shares (the PFE test turns on this).
How much Chinese-origin graphite is inside any US-bound shipment. Trade data has no lot-level tracing.
Why battery-maker shipments in our results stop after Aug 2025: data lag, a policy response or a change of route are all possible.

passport.paper_trail: Anode material shipped from Kendal and Morowali, Indonesia (HS 3801.10).
passport.note: The field covers the battery, not its anode.

passport.paper_trail: Artificial graphite from BTR Indonesia, whose inputs include HS 3801 from China and natural flake from Mozambique and Madagascar.
passport.note: Composition says what, not where from.

passport.note: Consistent, if declared.

caveats: Processing Chinese inputs in a third country is legal and common. Nothing here shows wrongdoing by any company named.
The US buyers are named because they appear in customs records; this says nothing about their compliance.
Entity-resolution links are our judgment and could be wrong.
HS 3801.10 also covers non-battery graphite (electrodes, refractories). Grain-size wording on some rows suggests industrial use.
Trade data has gaps: Indonesian export coverage is partial and dates may lag.
items.summary_for_non_experts: BTR is China's biggest maker of battery anode material. In 2024 it opened a large anode plant in Indonesia. Sayari's trade records show Chinese graphite going into that plant and graphite coming out of it to five US battery and car makers. What the records don't show is who owns the plant, which is the question US tax-credit rules now turn on.

items.title: BTR's Tangier anode plant
items.subtitle: BTR Mediterranean New Material Technology · Tanger Tech City, Morocco
items.question: Could Sayari detect Chinese graphite anode material reaching the US through BTR's new plant in Morocco, or through the Morocco–US graphite corridor?
items.headline: The reverse of Case 1: ownership is visible, trade is not. Sayari traces BTR's Moroccan subsidiary to BTR in China through a Singapore holding company, 100% at each step. The plant has no graphite trade yet, and the 3,088 'graphite' shipments from Morocco to the US are mostly mislabelled fertilizers and chemicals, plus a little European industrial graphite.
items.summary_for_non_experts: BTR, the world's biggest maker of graphite for battery anodes, is building a 60,000-tonne-a-year anode plant near Tangier through a local subsidiary. Morocco has a US free-trade agreement, so a plant there could one day supply US battery makers. Sayari's company records show that the plant belongs to BTR, via Singapore and a BTR subsidiary in Jiangsu. So far the plant has only imported building materials and machinery from China. None of the large Morocco-to-US 'graphite' trade is battery material.

key_numbers.label: BTR's indirect stake in BTR Mediterranean, at each of three registry steps (Morocco → Singapore → Jiangsu → BTR)
graphite shipments in or out of the Moroccan plant's six Sayari records
Morocco → US rows coded as artificial graphite (HS 3801.10) since Jan 2024
sampled corridor rows that are really fertilizer, pesticide or chemicals
real graphite rows found, all industrial (SGL Carbon, GrafTech, Resonac)

steps.title: The plant: two companies, six records
steps.text: Sayari holds two Moroccan BTR companies, registered in Oct 2023 and May 2024, and four customs-data fragments. One fragment shares the registry address (Lot 25, Tanger Tech), so we merge it as Inferred. The other three match by name only and stay leads.

steps.title: The owner: visible this time
steps.text: Moroccan records name a Singapore holding company, BNUO International, as 100% owner. Singapore records show BNUO is 100% owned by BTR (Jiangsu), and Chinese records show BTR owns all of BTR (Jiangsu). One step is a 'possibly same as' link between two BNUO records, backed by a shared officer. BTR's own release confirms the subsidiary.

steps.title: Inputs: steel and machinery, not graphite
steps.text: All 10 shipment rows for the plant are inbound from China, Nov 2025 – Jun 2026: pipes, racks, machinery and goods from a construction contractor. There is no graphite in and nothing out. The plant is still being built.

steps.title: The corridor: a mislabelled bucket
steps.text: The 3,088 Morocco-to-US artificial graphite rows are led by fertilizer, pesticide and oil firms such as Haifa Negev, Coromandel, Gandhar, Rotem Amfert and ADAMA. The main buyers are in Colombia, Mexico and Ecuador. Most rows describe fertilizer bags or chemical drums, and many share the same few arrival dates. This looks like a data error, not graphite trade.

steps.title: The real graphite is industrial
steps.text: The real graphite on the route is European electrode and rod stock: SGL Carbon (France to its US arm), GrafTech (Switzerland to GrafTech USA) and one Resonac electrode to a Mexican steelmaker. Sizes are in millimetres and inches, so it is industrial grade, not anode powder. Sayari shows no Morocco-to-US shipments from BTR, Gotion, CNGR/COBCO, Hailiang or Shinzoom.

detected.text: A registry ownership chain from BTR New Material Group to BTR Mediterranean New Material Technology: BTR → BTR (Jiangsu) → BNUO International Holding (Singapore) → the Moroccan company, 100% at each step.
A second Moroccan company, BTR Mediterranean Anode New Material Technology, 100% owned by Rian International Holding (Singapore), whose shareholder is a Singapore record of BTR.
Construction-stage imports from China to the plant (pipes, racks, machinery), Nov 2025 – Jun 2026.

The Morocco-to-US HS 3801.10 bucket is dominated by mislabelled fertilizer, pesticide and chemical cargo for Latin American buyers. The real graphite in it is industrial (SGL Carbon, GrafTech, Resonac).

suggested.text: One executive appears to run the Moroccan company, the Singapore holding company and BTR (Jiangsu). This is a name match across English and Chinese records.
The four trade fragments belong to the two registry companies; one by shared address, three by name only.

not_visible.text: Any graphite going into or out of the Moroccan plant. It has not started production, so there is no trail yet.
Which of the two Moroccan companies will run the anode line and which the cathode line.
Any Chinese-owned battery-material exporter on the Morocco-to-US route.

passport.declared: The cell plant's location.
passport.paper_trail: No anode shipments from Morocco yet. Anode material from Tangier would appear as HS 3801.10 from MAR.
passport.note: The Morocco HS 3801.10 bucket is so noisy that a future anode flow would be hard to spot without naming the shipper.

passport.declared: 'Graphite' as the anode active material.
passport.paper_trail: Not yet observable: the plant has no graphite inputs or outputs in Sayari.
passport.note: The feedstock source (Chinese coke or graphite, or another source) is unknown until imports start.

passport.declared: Natural graphite listed if present.
passport.paper_trail: No graphite inputs recorded.
passport.note: Trail not started.

passport.declared: Deferred under the EU Battery Regulation.
passport.paper_trail: Both Moroccan companies carry 'possibly owned by a Sheffield Hallam-named entity' flags, through BTR.
passport.note: Ownership-based flags exist before any product does.

passport.declared: No such field in the EU passport.
passport.paper_trail: Registry chain: BTR (China) → BTR (Jiangsu) → BNUO (Singapore) → BTR Mediterranean (Morocco), 100% at each step.
passport.note: Here the PFE ownership question can be answered from registry data, unlike Case 1.

red_flags.flag: Chinese parent ownership of the transit plant
red_flags.note: 100% registry chain via Singapore; one 'possibly same as' step, backed by a shared officer.

red_flags.flag: Same HS imported from China and exported to the US
red_flags.note: No graphite in or out yet; the plant is under construction.

red_flags.flag: Recent incorporation vs. first export date
red_flags.note: Incorporated Oct 2023 and May 2024; no exports to compare.

red_flags.flag: Volume spike after a policy date
red_flags.note: Corridor date clusters (Jun–Jul 2025) come from mislabelled rows, not graphite.

red_flags.flag: Shared address or officer with a flagged entity
red_flags.note: One executive appears at the Moroccan, Singapore and Jiangsu companies; BNUO sits at a mass-registration address.

red_flags.flag: Entity-resolution fragmentation
red_flags.note: Two legal entities plus four trade fragments; BTR also has a separate Singapore record.

red_flags.flag: Forced-labor / UFLPA sub-tier flags
red_flags.note: Ownership-path flags via BTR (Sheffield Hallam); context, not a finding.

caveats: Building a plant in Morocco with Chinese ownership is legal and common. Nothing here shows wrongdoing by any company named.
The fertilizer, chemical and graphite companies are named because they appear in the HS 3801.10 bucket. Most appear only because of an apparent coding error in one trade data source.
We read about 90 of the 3,088 corridor rows (ranked results), not all of them. A small battery-grade flow could still be hidden in the rest.
'Departure Morocco' probably often means transshipment through Tanger Med; the European graphite rows likely did not originate in Morocco.
Entity-resolution links are our judgment and could be wrong. The shared-executive match is across scripts (English and Chinese records).
Sayari free-text queries rank rows but do not filter them; counts after a quoted query are not counts of matches.

items.title: Zhongke's Oman anode plant
items.subtitle: Zhongke Electric / Zhongke Shinzoom · Sohar Freezone, Oman
items.question: Could Sayari detect Chinese anode material reaching US buyers through Zhongke Electric's new plant in Oman, before and after it starts producing?
items.headline: Not yet: the trail hasn't started. Sayari has no record of the Sohar plant and no shipments into or out of it. The ownership chain is half visible. Sayari's Chinese registry shows Zhongke Electric owning the anode producer, and the company's own filing names the Hong Kong subsidiary that is building the plant. Today Zhongke graphite reaches the US mostly indirectly, through Malaysian cell plants, and only rarely direct from China.
items.summary_for_non_experts: Zhongke Electric is a Chinese company and one of China's top three anode makers. It is building a 200,000-tonne-a-year anode plant in Oman. Ground was broken on 8 May 2026, and first output is due in 2027. Because no anode leaves the plant yet, there is nothing to trace, but we mapped who owns it and how the company's anode material reaches the US now. Sayari shows China's registry chain and the Hong Kong company's existence. It does not show the Hong Kong-to-Oman link, which comes from the company's own stock-exchange filing.

key_numbers.label: Sayari records for the Oman plant or its project company
planned capacity, two phases; ground broken 8 May 2026
direct China→US shipment rows from Zhongke Shinzoom entities (2021–2025)
artificial-graphite rows to two Malaysian cell plants, Apr 2025–Apr 2026
existing 'Oman→US' HS 3801 rows, mostly Indian cargo relayed through Oman: noise

steps.title: The plant isn't in the data yet
steps.text: We searched in English and Chinese for any Zhongke, Shinzoom or Sohar anode entity in Oman, and for shipments into Oman under the group's name. Nothing came back. That fits a plant that broke ground in May 2026 and won't produce until 2027. The project company named in the filing has no Sayari record, so it appears here without a Sayari ID.

steps.title: The owner: registry in China, filing beyond it
steps.text: Sayari's registry data shows Zhongke Electric holding 100% of a Xingcheng holding company, which holds 99.998% of the anode producer, Hunan Zhongke Star City Graphite. The company's June 2025 filing says that producer owns 100% of Zhongke Shinzoom (HK) Holdings, which set up the Oman project company. Sayari has the Hong Kong company (formed Nov 2024) but no path from it to Zhongke Electric.

steps.title: The groundbreaking checks out
steps.text: The 8 May 2026 groundbreaking was a single-source claim. Now the company's website, Gulf News (citing Oman's news agency), MEED, Sina Finance and Baidu all report it. The Hong Kong investor's address in the filing matches a Sayari trade record that has already shipped to a US importer, so the vehicle is already active in trade.

steps.title: Today's baseline: mostly via Malaysia
steps.text: Direct China→US rows are few: 7 to SK Battery America (2021–22), 1 to GM (Mar 2025) and 1 to Chemico (Oct 2025). Since 2025, 32 rows of artificial graphite have gone to EVE Energy Malaysia and Linergy Power. Both ship lithium-ion cells to US buyers such as Eaton, Milwaukee Tool and Briggs & Stratton. Trade data can't show whether those cells contain Zhongke graphite.

steps.title: What to watch once Sohar starts
steps.text: The 'Oman→US artificial graphite' corridor already shows 917 rows, mostly Indian chemicals and freight relayed through Omani ports. A corridor filter won't spot the new plant; a buyer must watch named shippers. Watch for: the Sohar project company or Shinzoom (HK) Holdings as shipper; HS 3801 or petroleum coke moving from Zhongke's Chinese units into Sohar; and an Omani registry record naming the Hong Kong parent.

detected.text: Registry chain inside China: Zhongke Electric → (100%) Xingcheng holding company → (99.998%) Hunan Zhongke Star City Graphite.
Zhongke Shinzoom (HK) Holdings exists (incorporated 8 Nov 2024) and, under a matching address, appears as shipper of artificial graphite from China to Chemico LLC (Oct 2025).
Current flows: 9 direct China→US rows (SK Battery America, GM, Chemico) and 32 rows to Malaysian cell plants that ship cells to US buyers.

suggested.text: The Hong Kong → Oman ownership: stated in Zhongke's filing and Gulf press, not in Sayari.
Trade records 'Hunan Zhongke Shinzoom' and 'Shinzoom (HK) Holdings' are the registry companies, matched by street address.
Malaysian route: Zhongke graphite into EVE Energy Malaysia and Linergy Power, whose cells go to US buyers. The anode content of those cells can't be shown.

not_visible.text: The Oman plant itself: no entity, no inputs and no outputs in Sayari.
Any registry link from the Hong Kong vehicle to its Chinese parent or its Omani subsidiary.
Equipment or feedstock shipments into Sohar reported in Chinese press.

passport.paper_trail: Today: Ningxiang/Changsha, China, sometimes routed through Hong Kong. From 2027: possibly Sohar, Oman.
passport.note: An Oman origin label would hide a Chinese-owned producer.

passport.declared: 'Graphite' as the anode active material.
passport.paper_trail: Artificial graphite (HS 3801.10/3801.90) from Zhongke Shinzoom to Malaysian cell plants.
passport.note: Composition says what, not who made it.

passport.declared: Natural graphite listed if present.
passport.paper_trail: The rows we saw are artificial graphite. No natural-graphite inputs pulled.
passport.note: Consistent, if declared.

passport.declared: Deferred under the EU Battery Regulation.
passport.paper_trail: No forced-labor flag on Shinzoom's trade record. Two sister plants carry 'owned-by' flags through a co-owner.
passport.note: Flags sit on neighbours, not on the exporter.

passport.declared: No such field in the EU passport.
passport.paper_trail: Oman plant → HK Holdings → Hunan Zhongke Star City Graphite → Zhongke Electric (filing + registry).
passport.note: The US PFE test turns on this chain; half of it is outside Sayari.

red_flags.note: Registry shows the Chinese links; the HK→Oman links come from the company filing.

red_flags.flag: Same HS imported from China and exported to the US
red_flags.note: The plant has no trade yet.

red_flags.note: HK vehicle formed Nov 2024; shipper on a US entry by Oct 2025 (goods from China).

red_flags.note: Too few US rows to test. The Malaysian rows start in Apr 2025.

red_flags.flag: Shared address or officer with a flagged entity
red_flags.note: Watchlist hits run through index-fund and HKSCC shareholders: noise.

red_flags.note: Trade and registry records split; a dormant 2017 HK namesake.

red_flags.note: None on Shinzoom; 'owned-by' flags on two sister plants via a co-owner.

caveats: Building a plant abroad and processing Chinese inputs there is legal and common. Nothing here shows wrongdoing by any company named.
Buyers are named because they appear in customs records. That says nothing about their compliance.
The Hong Kong → Oman ownership comes from Zhongke's filing and press, not from a registry Sayari holds.
Address-based links between trade records and registry companies are our judgment and could be wrong.
Malaysian cell exports can't be tied to Zhongke graphite at the lot level.
Oman→US HS 3801.10 data is dominated by relayed Indian cargo and likely miscoding. Don't read the corridor as anode trade.
The US anti-dumping case named Zhongke Shinzoom entities at 93.50%, but the USITC's negative vote (Mar 2026) means no order took effect.

items.title: POSCO Future M: Korean owner, Chinese graphite
items.subtitle: POSCO Future M Co., Ltd. · Sejong and Pohang, South Korea
items.question: Could Sayari tell a non-Chinese-owned anode supplier that uses Chinese graphite apart from a Chinese-owned one?
items.headline: Yes on ownership, partly on inputs. Sayari's Korean registry data shows POSCO Holdings owns 58.2% of POSCO Future M, with no Chinese owner anywhere up the chain. It also shows Chinese natural graphite going in (to Dec 2023) and 95 anode shipments going out to GM, SK Battery America, Tesla, Panasonic and XALT (Dec 2021 – Jul 2026). It cannot show how much Chinese graphite ends up in any US-bound shipment, and its Chinese input trail stops in Dec 2023, while the company says it still uses Chinese spherical graphite.
items.summary_for_non_experts: POSCO Future M is the battery-materials arm of Korea's POSCO steel group. It is the largest anode maker outside China and sells to US battery and car plants. This is our contrast case: the owner is Korean, but the company has relied on China for spherical graphite, the rounded, purified graphite that natural-graphite anode is made from. Sayari shows the Korean owner clearly, unlike BTR's Indonesian plant in Case 1, and it shows Chinese graphite going in and anode going out to the US. What it cannot show is how much Chinese material is inside the anode that reaches the US.

key_numbers.label: stake held by POSCO Holdings (Korean registry record)
Chinese owners among 50 ownership paths
shipment rows of anode material to US battery and car makers, Dec 2021 – Jul 2026
China → Korea 'spherical graphite' shipments with POSCO Future M as buyer; latest 8 Dec 2023

steps.title: One company, one registry anchor
steps.text: Sayari holds about a dozen records for POSCO Future M under its old and new names. The main one carries Korea's DART disclosure ID, so the anchor is solid. Other records share its Pohang or Gwangyang street address; two are name-only and kept as leads.

steps.title: The owner is in the registry
steps.text: Korea's disclosure data, as held by Sayari, names POSCO Holdings as owner of 58.2%. Every other shareholder is Korean, including the National Pension Service. This is the question the US PFE rules ask first, and here Sayari answers it directly. In Case 1 it could not.

steps.title: Chinese graphite in
steps.text: Natural graphite (HS 2504) arrived from Zhanjiang Juxin and three Qingdao suppliers in 2023, and artificial graphite (HS 3801) from Qingdao Kuntuo and Qingdao Qingbei Carbon. POSCO Future M is the top Korean buyer of Chinese 'spherical graphite' in Sayari, with 167 shipments. Smaller inputs came from Mozambique, Germany and the UK.

steps.title: Anode out to US plants
steps.text: 105 shipment rows of HS 3801 left Korea for the US. 95 went to battery or car makers: GM (37), SK Battery America (32), Tesla (13), Panasonic Energy (9) and XALT Energy (4). The rest went to freight forwarders and one electrode maker. The company has also announced an anode deal with Ultium Cells, but Sayari's rows name GM as the consignee.

steps.title: What the data can't separate
steps.text: Trade rows can't link a Chinese input to a US-bound export, or tell Sejong's natural-graphite anode from Pohang's artificial-graphite anode. Chinese graphite rows to POSCO Future M stop on 8 Dec 2023, a week after China's export licensing began. The company says it still uses Chinese spherical graphite, so the gap is in coverage. Several name-and-HS searches returned 0 even though the graph holds the flows.

detected.text: Korean ownership: POSCO Holdings holds 58.2% (registry record); no Chinese owner on any of 50 ownership paths.
Chinese natural and artificial graphite shipped into POSCO Future M by named Chinese suppliers, Oct 2021 – Dec 2023.
95 dated rows of anode material to GM, SK Battery America, Tesla, Panasonic Energy and XALT Energy, Dec 2021 – Jul 2026.

suggested.text: Continued dependence on Chinese spherical graphite after 2023: stated by the company in the press, not visible in Sayari after 8 Dec 2023.
Anode supply to Ultium Cells: announced by the company; Sayari shows the shipments under GM's name.

not_visible.text: How much Chinese-origin graphite is inside any US-bound shipment. This is the 'material assistance' share the PFE rules weigh, separately from ownership.
Which plant (Sejong natural, Pohang artificial) made each US shipment. Product codes such as PAS-C3B and PAS-CP3K are not explained in the data.
Who the Chinese graphite suppliers are owned by. We did not trace them; under the PFE rules that could matter more than POSCO's own ownership.

passport.declared: The cell plant's location, e.g. USA.
passport.paper_trail: Anode material shipped from Korea (Pohang/Sejong) to US cell plants (HS 3801).
passport.note: The field covers the battery, not its anode.

passport.declared: 'Graphite' as the anode active material.
passport.paper_trail: Natural-graphite anode from Chinese spherical graphite (Sejong) or artificial-graphite anode from Korean coke (Pohang); the rows don't say which.
passport.note: Two very different input chains look the same here.

passport.declared: Natural graphite listed if present.
passport.paper_trail: Natural graphite (HS 2504) from China and Mozambique among the inputs.
passport.note: Consistent, if declared.

passport.declared: Deferred under the EU Battery Regulation.
passport.paper_trail: Sub-tier suppliers in the Laixi graphite cluster; one carries a forced-labor-adjacent flag.
passport.note: The upstream suppliers are visible; their own sourcing is not.

passport.declared: No such field in the EU passport.
passport.paper_trail: The anode maker is Korean-owned (registry). Its graphite suppliers are Chinese companies whose owners we did not trace.
passport.note: The PFE test looks at both levels.

red_flags.flag: Chinese parent ownership of the transit plant
red_flags.note: Checked and absent: the registry shows a Korean parent (POSCO Holdings, 58.2%).

red_flags.flag: Same HS imported from China and exported to the US
red_flags.note: HS 3801 in from Qingdao suppliers (2021–2023); HS 3801 out to US cell plants. Normal for a processor; the main input is natural graphite (HS 2504).

red_flags.flag: Recent incorporation vs. first export date
red_flags.note: Checked and absent: registered 1971, decades before its first anode exports.

red_flags.note: No spike in our rows. The buyer mix shifts: GM to Jun 2024, SK Battery America to Jun 2025, Tesla and Panasonic in 2026.

red_flags.flag: Shared address or officer with a flagged entity
red_flags.note: None found. Watchlist hits are two hops out through big trading partners (noise).

caveats: Using Chinese graphite in Korea is legal and common. Nothing here shows wrongdoing by any company named.
The US buyers are named because they appear in customs records; this says nothing about their compliance.
Entity-resolution links are our judgment and could be wrong.
HS 3801 also covers non-battery graphite. POSCO's sister steel company imports Chinese 'recarburizer' under HS 3801.10, a steelmaking additive; we excluded it.
Chinese input rows come from Chinese export data and stop in Dec 2023 for this buyer. Korea's own import records are not in our results, so later inputs may be missing.
Several product rows are miscoded (e.g. anode material under textile or photo-film HS codes); we counted them only where the text says anode material.

items.title: Putailai's Zichen anode plant in Malaysia
items.subtitle: Zichen Malaysia Sdn. Bhd. · Gurun, Kedah, Malaysia
items.question: Could corridor scans of US graphite imports from Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand, Mexico and Korea find a Chinese-owned anode plant shipping to the US?
items.headline: Not yet. In five corridors we found no Chinese-owned anode maker shipping artificial graphite to the US. The rows were electrode makers, machined graphite parts, forwarders and mislabelled chemicals. The one Chinese-owned anode plant in these countries, Putailai's Zichen Malaysia, is clear in the registry: 100% owned through Singapore by Shanghai Putailai. But it is still being built and has no trade.
items.summary_for_non_experts: We scanned US import records of artificial graphite from five countries where Chinese anode makers might set up. None showed a Chinese-owned anode producer selling to US battery plants. The only Chinese-owned anode plant in those countries is Putailai's 50,000-tonne plant in Kedah, Malaysia, which broke ground in June 2026. Unlike Case 1, the registry shows exactly who owns it, so if it ever ships to the US, the ownership question that decides US tax credits will already be answered.

steps.title: Five corridors, no Chinese anode maker
steps.text: Since January 2024, US imports of artificial graphite (HS 3801.10) came from 347 suppliers in Mexico, 107 in Korea, 8 in Thailand, 5 in Vietnam and 2 in Malaysia. Mexico's leaders are electrode makers and chemical firms. Korea's are POSCO and Japanese-owned carbon makers. Vietnam's top shipper sends machined graphite jigs. Thailand's are mostly forwarders.

steps.title: Where 'anode' does show up
steps.text: Searching row descriptions for 'anode' found 398 US-bound rows, none from Vietnam, Malaysia or Thailand. Mexico's and Oman's 'anode' rows are mislabelled chemicals. Singapore is different: 'carbon anode materials' reached General Motors, L-H Battery and NextStar Energy in Aug–Sep 2026 with no producer named. The only named shipper was an Indonesian forwarder.

steps.title: The plant: registered, not yet shipping
steps.text: Zichen Malaysia Sdn. Bhd. was registered on 23 Sep 2025 to make battery materials and carbon products. Press reports put its 50,000-tonne anode plant in Gurun, Kedah, with ground broken on 1 June 2026 and about two years of building ahead. Sayari shows no trade in or out.

steps.title: The owner: in the registry this time
steps.text: Malaysian shareholder data lists Putailai (Singapore) as owning 100% of Zichen Malaysia. Sayari's ownership graph links that company to the Shanghai-listed Putailai group, and Putailai's own announcement calls Zichen Malaysia a wholly owned subsidiary. Two directors share names with group shareholders. That is a lead, not a link.

steps.title: A trail that hasn't started
steps.text: With no trade, we can't show inputs from China or buyers in the US. A name search for the group's existing exports returned only unrelated 'Zichen' firms. Two boolean searches returned nothing. The plant is a watch item: its first export rows will show whether its graphite reaches US cell plants.

caveats: Building a plant abroad is legal and common. Nothing here shows wrongdoing by any company named.
US buyers and corridor shippers are named because they appear in customs records; this says nothing about their compliance.
HS 3801.10 is noisy: many corridor rows are mis-coded chemicals, electrodes or machined parts. Supplier counts overstate battery trade.
Facet scans count suppliers, not tonnes. A corridor with few suppliers can still carry large volumes.
Sayari's Malaysian ownership data comes from a third-party shareholder source; stake percentages above the Singapore level were not returned.
Name matches between directors and parent shareholders are leads only.
